Abstract
    

Suppose a graph has no large balanced bicliques, but has large minimum degree. Then what can we say about its induced subgraphs? This question motivates the study of degree-boundedness, which is like χ\chi-boundedness but for minimum degree instead of chromatic number. We survey this area with an eye towards open problems.

1 Introduction




Informally, a class of graphs ℱ\mathcal{F} is degree-bounded if every graph in ℱ\mathcal{F} with sufficiently large minimum degree has a big balanced biclique Kt,tK_{t,t} as a subgraph. This intuitively says that for graphs in ℱ\mathcal{F}, minimum degree is a “local property”. This is definitely not the case for all graphs due to a famous random construction of Erdős [51] and lower bounds on the Kővári-Sós-Turán Theorem [85] on the extremal numbers of bipartite graphs. In fact, degree-boundedness has many nice connections to extremal graph theory, and we discuss these in Section 2.




For now though, we focus on what has recently become the standard definition of degree-boundedness. Given a graph GG, the biclique number of GG is the largest integer tt so that GG has a subgraph (not necessarily induced) which is isomorphic to the biclique Kt,tK_{t,t}. We denote the biclique number of GG by τ⁡(G)\tau(G). Then a class of graphs ℱ\mathcal{F} is degree-bounded if there exists a function ff so that each graph G∈ℱG\in\mathcal{F} has a vertex of degree at most f⁡(τ⁡(G))f(\tau(G)).
